faqs.a: A focused marketing site is typically 3–5 weeks. Larger corporate platforms with a CMS and multiple languages run 8–12 weeks.

faqs.q: How long until we see results?
faqs.a: Technical and on-page wins can show within 4–8 weeks. Competitive content and authority gains typically take 4–6 months to mature.

faqs.q: Do you guarantee #1 rankings?
faqs.a: No credible SEO does. We commit to a defined scope of work and report transparently on rankings, traffic and conversions.

faqs.q: Can you implement the fixes or just advise?
faqs.a: We can do both. Many clients have us implement directly; others want us to brief their dev team. Your call.

faqs.q: Is link building safe?
faqs.a: Yes — we only pursue editorially earned links from relevant sites. We never buy links from networks or use private blog networks.

blogs.title: Core Web Vitals in 2026: a practical checklist
blogs.author: Priya Nair
blogs.excerpt: What actually moves LCP, INP and CLS on real projects — and the measurement mistakes that hide regressions.
blogs.body:
Core Web Vitals reward the same things good engineering always has: send less, send it sooner, and do not shift the layout under the user. This post is the checklist we run on every build.

## Largest Contentful Paint

Preload the hero image and font, serve modern formats, and make sure the LCP element is not lazy-loaded. On most sites, an unoptimised hero image is the single biggest offender.

## Interaction to Next Paint

Break up long tasks, defer non-critical JavaScript, and keep third-party tags on a leash. Measure with a real device, not a fast laptop.

## Cumulative Layout Shift

- Always set width and height on media
- Reserve space for embeds and ads
- Avoid inserting content above existing content

blogs.title: React Native vs native: how we actually decide
blogs.author: Daniel Osei
blogs.excerpt: A decision framework for choosing between React Native and fully native — beyond the usual talking points.
blogs.body:
The honest answer is “it depends”, but the dependencies are predictable. Here is the framework we use with clients.

## Choose React Native when

- You need iOS and Android from one team
- The UI is mostly standard components and lists
- Time to market matters more than squeezing the last 5% of performance

## Choose native when

- You need heavy graphics, AR or camera pipelines
- Deep OS integration is core to the product
- You already have strong native teams

blogs.title: The real trade-offs of going headless
blogs.author: Priya Nair
blogs.excerpt: Headless CMS gives you flexibility and speed — at the cost of more moving parts. When it is worth it.
blogs.body:
Headless is not automatically better. It is a trade: you gain a clean content API and front-end freedom, and you take on preview infrastructure, build pipelines and more services to run.

## Good fit

Content-heavy sites, multi-channel content, teams that want a modern front-end stack, and projects where performance is a KPI.

## Poor fit

Small brochure sites with one editor and no performance pressure — a well-configured traditional CMS ships faster.

blogs.title: How to write an SEO content brief writers do not hate
blogs.author: Marcus Feld
blogs.excerpt: A brief template that gives writers intent, structure and sources without turning them into keyword-stuffing machines.
blogs.body:
A good brief answers three questions: who is searching this, what do they need to walk away with, and what proof should the article include?

## What belongs in the brief

- Primary query and the intent behind it
- Target reader and their level of knowledge
- Outline with H2/H3 suggestions
- Sources, data points and internal links to include
- What “done” looks like

blogs.title: Automating the back office without a big-bang project
blogs.author: Elena Rossi
blogs.excerpt: How to sequence automation so each release pays for the next, instead of betting everything on one launch.
blogs.body:
The failure mode for internal software is the 12-month project that launches all at once. Sequencing by value avoids it.

## The sequence

- Instrument the current process to get a baseline
- Automate the single most painful step first
- Ship it, measure hours saved, use that to fund the next step
- Only then integrate adjacent systems

blogs.title: Paid media tracking that survives privacy changes
blogs.author: Marcus Feld
blogs.excerpt: Server-side tagging, consent mode and first-party data — a pragmatic setup for reliable conversion tracking.
blogs.body:
Browser-side pixels are a shrinking signal. A durable setup leans on server-side events and your own first-party data.

## The stack we use

- Server-side GTM for event collection
- Consent mode configured properly
- Offline conversion imports for long sales cycles
- A clean data layer as the single source

blogs.title: Design systems for small teams: how light is too light?
blogs.author: Priya Nair
blogs.excerpt: You do not need a 300-component library. You need tokens, a dozen primitives and the discipline to use them.
blogs.body:
For a team of five, a full design system is overhead. A “design kit” — tokens plus a small set of primitives — gets 80% of the benefit.

## The minimum viable kit

- Colour, spacing, radius and type tokens
- Button, Input, Card, Modal, Tabs
- One documented layout grid
- A usage doc, not a Storybook cathedral

blogs.title: Shipping accessible interfaces by default
blogs.author: Daniel Osei
blogs.excerpt: Accessibility is cheap when it is a habit and expensive when it is an audit. Build the habits into your components.
blogs.body:
Most accessibility issues trace back to a handful of components. Fix them once, at the primitive level, and every page inherits the fix.

## High-leverage fixes

- Focus-visible styles on every interactive element
- Labels tied to inputs, errors announced
- Modal focus trap and escape handling
- Colour contrast checked in the token palette
